function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to help you set up the infrastructure for your **nodejs‑welcome** project, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone repositories, run `git` commands, or push commits back to GitHub from here.  
What I *can* do is generate the files you’ll need (Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests) for you to drop into the repo, and then give you step‑by‑step instructions on how to finish the rest locally.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository (locally)

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you’re not already authenticated with SSH keys, you’ll need to set those up first.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Generate Files

### 2.1 Create/Update Dockerfile

Assuming the repo contains a standard Node.js application (`app.js` or `index.js`) that listens on port 3000, we’ll generate a minimal Dockerfile:

```json
{
  "directory_name": ".",
  "base_image": "node:18-alpine",
  "maintainer": "Your Name <you@example.com>",
  "expose_port": 3000,
  "entrypoint": "node app.js"
}
```

Calling the tool:

```json
{
  "name": "create_a_docker_file",
  "arguments": {
    "directory_name": ".",
    "base_image": "node:18-alpine",
    "maintainer": "Your Name <you@example.com>",
    "expose_port": 3000,
    "entrypoint": "node app.js"
  }
}
```

> The tool will write a `Dockerfile` in the current directory with the above settings.

### 2.2 Create Kubernetes YAML

For a simple deployment exposing port 3000 and a LoadBalancer service:

```json
{
  "directory_name": ".",
  "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "image_name": "your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest",
  "replicas": 3,
  "port": 3000,
  "service_type": "LoadBalancer"
}
```

Calling the tool:

```json
{
  "name": "create_kubernetes_yaml_file",
  "arguments": {
    "directory_name": ".",
    "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome",
    "image_name": "your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    "replicas": 3,
    "port": 3000,
    "service_type": "LoadBalancer"
  }
}
```

> The tool will create two files: `k8s-deployment.yaml` and `k8s-service.yaml`.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

There’s no built‑in function for this, so you’ll need to create it yourself. A minimal CI that builds the Docker image and pushes it to Docker Hub (or GitHub Container Registry) would look like this:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
```

> Replace `your-docker-registry` with your actual registry (e.g., `docker.io/yourusername`).  
> Store your credentials in the repo’s **Settings → Secrets** as `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add Generated Files to Git

After the tools have written the files, stage them:

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml k8s-service.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

If you want to overwrite an existing Dockerfile or Kubernetes files, just `git add` them again – Git will detect the changes.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That’s it! Your repo now contains:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s-deployment.yaml` | Deploys 3 replicas of the app |
| `k8s-service.yaml` | Exposes the deployment via a LoadBalancer |
| `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` | Automates building & pushing the image on each push to `main` |

Feel free to tweak the generated files (e.g., change the base image, adjust replica count, or switch the service type). Once you push, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger and build your Docker image.
